Published in final edited form as: Arthritis Care Res (Hoboken). 2013 Oct;65(10):1600–1607. doi: 10.1002/acr.22039 Abstract BACKGROUND Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is associated with cardiovascular disease (CVD) but little is known about its association with another form of vascular disorder, venous thromboembolism (VTE). METHODS A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the US insurance claims. RA and non-RA patients were matched on age, sex, and index date. Incidence rates (IR) and rate ratios (RR) of VTE, defined as the composite of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE), were calculated. Cox proportional hazards models compared VTE risks between RA and non-RA patients, adjusting for VTE risk factors such as CVD, surgery, hospitalization, medications, and acute phase reactants (APR). RESULTS Over the mean follow-up of 2 years, the IR for VTE among RA patients was 6.1 per 1,000 person-years, 2.4 times higher (95%CI 2.1–2.8) than the rate of non-RA patients. The IRs for both DVT (RR 2.2, 95%CI 1.9–2.6) and PE (RR 2.7, 95%CI 2.2–3.5) were higher in RA compared with non-RA patients. After adjusting for risk factors of VTE, the VTE risk remained elevated in RA (hazard ratio 1.4, 95%CI 1.1–1.7) compared to non-RA patients. The result was similar after further adjustment for elevated APR (hazard ratio 1.5, 95%CI 0.3–6.5). One-third of patients who developed VTE had at least one major VTE risk factors 90 days before and after the VTE event. CONCLUSION Our results showed an increased risk of developing VTE for RA patients compared with non-RA patients. The risk was attenuated but remained elevated even after adjusting for various risk factors for VTE. Other known risk factors for VTE are fracture of lower extremities, joint replacement surgery, major general surgery, major trauma, malignancy, heart or respiratory failure, pregnancy, history of VTE, hormone replacement therapy and oral contraceptive use, but do not traditionally include inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA).(2, 3) The link between chronic systemic inflammatory diseases, such as RA, and cardiovascular disease (CVD), including myocardial infarction and stroke, has been well documented.(4–7) Systemic inflammation may also play a important role in the development of VTE as inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-6, IL-8, and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) could modulate thrombotic responses by activating coagulation pathways.(8, 9) Markers of systemic inflammation, such as C-reactive protein (CRP), fibrinogen, and factor VIII, are also found at higher levels in patients with VTE, similar to atherothrombosis.(10, 11) Recent studies report that patients with RA have a 1.5- to 6-fold increased risk of VTE, such as pulmonary embolism (PE) and deep vein thrombosis (DVT) compared to non-RA patients.(12–18) Many of these studies identified their RA cohort based on a hospital discharge diagnosis of RA which could introduce a bias to select patients with severe RA and hence may not be generalizable to typical RA patients seen in the outpatient setting.(13–16) Furthermore, no prior studies have examined the VTE risk in RA adjusting for acute phase reactant levels. The objectives of this study are 1) to examine the rate of incident VTE in a cohort of patients with RA compared with those without RA in the general population, 2) to assess the VTE risk in RA compared to non-RA adjusting for a number of known risk factors for VTE as well as baseline acute phase reactant levels, and 3) to determine the proportion of VTE cases in the presence of major VTE risk factor such as recent hospitalization, surgery and malignancy during the follow-up period. METHODS Data Source We conducted a cohort study using the claims data from a commercial U.S. health plan which insures primarily working adults and their family members, and a small Medicare population for the period January 1, 2001 through June 30, 2008. Results for outpatient laboratory tests, including C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) were available on a subset of beneficiaries. fetched_contents.text: Venous thrombosis risk during and after medical and surgical hospitalizations: The medical inpatient thrombosis and hemostasis (MITH) study Abstract Background Thirty to seventy percent of all venous thromboembolism (VTE) events are associated with hospitalization. The absolute and relative risks during and after hospitalization are poorly characterized. Objectives Quantify the absolute rate and relative risk of VTE during and up to 3 months after medical and surgical hospitalizations. Patients/Methods We conducted an observational cohort study between 2010 and 2016 of patients cared for by the University of Vermont (UVM) Health Network's primary care population. Cox proportional hazard models with hospitalization modeled as a time‐varying covariate were used to estimate VTE risk. Results Over 4.3 years of follow‐up, 55 220 hospitalizations (156 per 1000 person‐years) and 713 first venous thromboembolism events (2.0 per 1000 person‐years) occurred. Among individuals not recently hospitalized, the rate of venous thromboembolism was 1.4 per 1000 person‐years and 71.8 per 1000 person‐years during hospitalization. During the first, second, and third months after discharge, the rates of venous thromboembolism were 35.1, 11.3, and 5.2 per 1000 person‐years, respectively. Relative to those not recently hospitalized, the age‐ and sex‐adjusted HRs of venous thromboembolism were 38.0 (95% CI 28.0, 51.5) during hospitalization, and 18.4 (95% CI 15.0, 22.6), 6.3 (95% CI 4.3, 9.0), and 3.0 (95% CI 1.7, 5.4) during the first, second, and third months after discharge, respectively. Stratified by medical versus surgical services the rates were similar. Conclusion Hospitalization and up to 3 months after discharge were strongly associated with increased venous thromboembolism risk. These data quantify this risk for use in future studies. Keywords: cohort studies, epidemiology, hospitalization, patient discharge, venous thromboembolism ---------------------------------------- Essentials. * Hospitalization is a key risk factor for Venous Thrombosis but little is known about the absolute and relative risk in a contemporary population. * We assessed hospitalization as a risk factor for VTE in a primary care population in northwest Vermont, United States. * Hospitalization resulted in a 38‐fold increased hazard of VTE, with risk remaining 3‐fold higher up to 3‐months after discharge. * We characterized the relative and absolute risk of VTE during and up to 3‐months after hospitalization which can be used to design further intervention studies. 1. To address the gap in contemporary knowledge of the relative and absolute contribution of hospitalization on VTE risk, we followed a cohort of individuals receiving primary care at sites affiliated with an academic medical center in Vermont. We sought to (1) determine the relative and absolute risk of VTE during and up to 3 months after hospitalization and (2) assess VTE risk by medical and surgical hospitalizations. 2. METHODS 2.1. Population Individuals 18 years old and older who received at least one primary care visit at the UVM Health Network were included in the cohort. UVM Medical Center is a tertiary care hospital in northwestern Vermont that serves as the primary (and only) hospital and imaging center for Chittenden County, VT with a population of 164 572 (Figure 1). 11 UVM Medical Center deployed the fully integrated Epic electronic medical record across its inpatient and ambulatory services in October 2010 (Epic Systems Corporation, Verona, WI). Thus, individuals receiving primary care with UVM providers have near complete capture of their healthcare utilization. Individuals with a past history of VTE defined per International Classification of Diseases, Ninth or Tenth Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD‐9/10‐CM) diagnosis codes occurring within the first 3 months of entry to the cohort were excluded from all analyses (codes listed in Tables S1 and S2). 12 2.2. fetched_contents.text: Hospital‐related first venous thromboembolism and risk of recurrence Introduction Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), collectively referred to as venous thromboembolism (VTE), are frequently associated with considerable morbidity and mortality 1., 2., 3.. VTE is particularly common among hospitalized patients, with incidence rates (IRs) exceeding 100 times greater than those in community residents 4. Moreover, 40–50% of the VTE cases can be attributed to hospitalization, with hospitalization for surgery and medical illness accounting for similar proportions 5. After an incident episode of VTE, 30–40% experience a recurrent event within 10 years, and the risk is highest during the first 6–12 months 2., 6., 7., 8., 9.. The risk of recurrence is dependent on the clinical characteristics of the initial event. Patients with a first VTE provoked by a transient risk factor (e.g. surgery) are at low risk of recurrence 6., 8., 10., 11., 12., 13., whereas VTEs provoked by a persistent risk factor, such as active cancer, have a high risk of recurrence 6., 8., 12., 14., 15.. When no provoking risk factor (transient or persistent) can be identified, the event is classified as unprovoked, and these patients have an intermediate to high risk of recurrence 9., 10., 11., 12., 13., 16., 17.. However, categorization along this continuum may be difficult, particularly for patients where considerable uncertainty exists regarding the prognostic importance of a risk factor. Hospitalization in itself is an interim exposure and may therefore be considered as a transient risk factor, assumed to yield a low risk of recurrence. However, the risk of recurrence after a first hospital‐related VTE, particularly hospitalization for conditions other than cancer or surgery, has not been extensively studied. Moreover, as the mortality rate is expected to be higher among patients with co‐morbidity, the cumulative incidence of recurrence may be influenced by the competing risk of death, particularly in these patients 18. In the present study, we therefore aimed to investigate the risk of recurrence and mortality among patients with a first hospital‐related VTE, and to compare the impact of transient and persistent hospital‐related factors such as surgery, cancer or other medical conditions on the risk of recurrence in models with and without death as a competing event. Methods Study population The source population comprised subjects participating in the first (1974), second (1979/80), third (1986/87), fourth (1994/95), fifth (2001/02) and sixth (2007/08) surveys of the Tromsø study. The Tromsø study is a single‐center, population‐based, prospective cohort study, with repeated health surveys of inhabitants in the municipality of Tromsø in the north of Norway. Further details about the Tromsø study can be found elsewhere 19. The Regional Committee of Medical and Health Research Ethics approved the study, and written consent was collected from all participants. Overall, 39 825 unique individuals, aged 25–97 years, participated in at least one of the surveys, which yielded an average participation rate of 78.5% for all surveys. Participants that were still alive and living in the municipality of Tromsø by 1 January 1994 (n = 33 885) were followed through to 31 December 2012, and all potential cases of first lifetime VTE were identified by searching the hospital discharge diagnosis registry, the autopsy registry and the radiology procedure registry at the University Hospital of North of Norway. This is the only hospital in the region and serves as the exclusive provider of all diagnostic radiology procedures and VTE‐related healthcare in the area. Trained personnel reviewed the medical records for each potential VTE case and extracted information for case‐validation. A VTE event was considered verified and recorded when presence of clinical signs and symptoms of DVT or PE were combined with objective confirmation tests (compression ultrasonography, venography, spiral computed tomography, perfusion‐ventilation scan, pulmonary angiography and autopsy) and resulted in a VTE diagnosis that required treatment, as previously described 20. Using the criteria described above, 822 subjects with a validated first lifetime VTE event were identified and included in our study. Patient characteristics Information on clinical and provoking factors at the time of and 8 weeks preceding the VTE event, were extracted by review of medical records using standardized forms. We defined a VTE as being hospital related when patients were hospitalized within 8 weeks preceding the VTE (including patients hospitalized at the time of VTE), had undergone surgery (with or without subsequent hospitalization) within 8 weeks preceding the event or had active cancer. When none of these factors could be identified, the event was classified as non‐hospital‐related. Cancer was registered as the provoking factor only when patients had active cancer at the time of the initial event. Bedrest was defined as confinement to bed in hospital > 3 days, whereas other immobilization was defined as transient or persistent use of a wheelchair or long haul travel > 4 h (i.e. by airplane, train, car or boat). Hospital‐related VTE was classified into three main categories according to the main provoking factor for the first VTE following the algorithm: cancer > surgery > hospitalization for other medical illness. Clinical factors included were obesity, use of estrogens, family history of VTE, pregnancy, puerperium or other co‐morbidities. Participants were classified as obese according to the World Health Organization definition (BMI > 30 kg m−2) 21. Co‐morbidity was defined as a myocardial infarction or a stroke within the last 12 months preceding the VTE, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), myeloproliferative disorders, systemic lupus erythematosus or a chronic infection. Acute hospitalization-related VTE risk and timing

Hospitalization is a well-established acute risk factor for venous thromboembolism (VTE), with the evidence base here showing that hospitalization itself can raise the risk dramatically. In the MITH study, hospitalization was associated with a 38-fold increased hazard of VTE compared with not recently hospitalized individuals, and the risk remained 3-fold higher up to 3 months after discharge [N2-F2]. This means that risk is not confined to the hospital stay alone: it peaks strongly during admission and then declines, but remains elevated for at least the first month or so after discharge [N2-F2].

During hospital stay, the risk is particularly elevated. The MITH study found that during hospitalization the VTE rate was 71.8 per 1000 person-years, versus 1.4 per 1000 person-years in the non-recency hospitalized comparator group [N2-F2]. The absolute risk is therefore very high while the patient is in the hospital. Over the first few months after discharge, the risk declines progressively: 35.1 per 1000 person-years in the first month, 11.3 per 1000 person-years in the second month, and 5.2 per 1000 person-years in the third month [N2-F2]. So the risk peaks immediately after admission and during hospitalization, then declines over time, but not back to baseline.

For hospitalized RA patients, several risk factors are specific and should be emphasized. The MITH study did not separate RA patients from others in its main analysis, but the broader evidence base here is that RA patients face additional VTE risk factors including smoking, obesity, major surgery, hospitalization with immobilization, and RA therapies [N4-R4]. In addition, RA itself is associated with chronic inflammation, which may contribute to VTE risk [N5-R4]. The study on RA and VTE specifically found that RA was associated with elevated VTE risk even after adjusting for major VTE risk factors such as hospitalization, surgery, and malignancy [N1-F1]. That means hospitalization is one of many important risk factors, but RA-related inflammation and comorbidity can make hospitalized RA patients especially vulnerable [N5-R3][N5-R4].

Hospitalized RA patients also face risk factors linked to immobilization and comorbid conditions. The evidence from RA and VTE reviews notes that established VTE risk factors such as age, immobilization, and comorbid conditions occur more frequently in RA patients [N5-R3]. The CDC’s general guidance on healthcare-associated VTE also states that people who are currently or recently hospitalized or recovering from surgery are at increased risk of serious blood clots [N2-R2]. This is relevant to hospitalized RA patients because they may have both the hospitalization exposure and the associated immobilization, comorbid conditions, and treatment burden that further elevate VTE risk [N5-R4][N4-R4].

Taken together, the risk pattern is clear: hospitalization itself is an acute, strong trigger for VTE, with the highest risk during hospital stay and a sharp decline thereafter. For hospitalized RA patients, the risk is further amplified by inflammation, immobilization, comorbid conditions, and treatment-related factors [N2-F2][N5-R3][N5-R4][N4-R4]. The evidence supports a model in which risk peaks early and then declines over time in hospital, rather than remaining constant or rising further [N2-F2].
node_outputs.N11:
Post-hospitalization follow-up and long-term VTE risk

The evidence shows that VTE risk does not end with discharge. After hospitalization, the risk remains elevated for weeks and months, and recurrence risk is notably higher in the early post-discharge period. In the Tromsø study, patients with a first hospital-related VTE had a high recurrence risk, and the risk of recurrence was highest during the first 6–12 months after the initial event [N3-F3]. A separate study found that recurrence risk was at least 6% within 2 years and continued to recur for at least 10 years after the first VTE [N7-R1]. This indicates that the post-discharge period is not a single acute event but a prolonged risk period.

Recurrence risk is especially high in the first few weeks and months after discharge. The Tromsø study notes that the risk of recurrence is highest during the first 6–12 months after the first VTE event [N3-F3]. A general AFP review also states that the long-term risk of symptomatic recurrent VTE after discontinuation of anticoagulant treatment is substantial, with one third of people with a VTE having a recurrence within 10 years and one third to one half having a recurrence after a DVT [N3-R5]. In the context of post-hospitalization follow-up, this means the first several months after discharge are a critical window for recurrence. A study on post-discharge treatment patterns also defines recurrent VTE as any hospitalization with a primary diagnosis of VTE occurring at least 7 days after the first discharge date [N3-R4], reinforcing that recurrence can occur soon after discharge.

Beyond 1 year, the long-term risk continues to accumulate and may plateau or remain elevated. The AFP review reports that recurrence risk is highest during the first 6–12 months and continues for at least 10 years after the initial event [N3-R5]. A 2020 study on recurrence after a first venous thromboembolic event found cumulative recurrence probabilities of 10.9% after 2 years, 29% after 10 years, and 56% after 20 years [N7-R5]. This shows that long-term risk is substantial and does not simply decline sharply after the first year. The evidence also suggests that recurrence risk may plateau or remain elevated over decades, rather than falling to a negligible baseline [N7-R5].

The impact of continued inflammation, treatment, and lifestyle factors is important. The evidence on RA and VTE indicates that chronic inflammation is likely a major contributor to the association between RA and VTE [N5-R4]. In hospitalized RA patients, RA-related inflammation, immobilization, and comorbid conditions are repeatedly cited as important risk factors [N5-R3][N5-R4]. The general VTE literature also emphasizes that recurrence risk depends on the clinical characteristics of the initial event, with persistent risk factors such as active cancer associated with higher recurrence [N3-F3]. In the context of post-hospitalization follow-up, this means that inflammation, treatment burden, comorbid conditions, and lifestyle factors may all contribute to ongoing risk [N5-R4][N5-R3][N3-F3]. For RA patients, continued disease activity is also associated with higher VTE risk, reinforcing that inflammation is a relevant ongoing contributor [N8-R2].

In summary, post-hospitalization VTE risk is highest during the first few weeks and months after discharge, declines progressively over time, but remains substantial for years. Long-term recurrence risk continues beyond 1 year and may plateau or accumulate over decades. Inflammation, treatment, and lifestyle factors all play a role, especially in RA patients where chronic inflammation appears to be a key driver [N3-F3][N3-R5][N7-R5][N5-R4][N8-R2].
node_outputs.N9:
Baseline VTE risk associated with rheumatoid arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is associated with an elevated baseline VTE risk compared with controls, with both absolute and relative risk estimates consistently higher than in non-RA populations. The RA-VTE cohort study reported that the incidence rate (IR) of VTE among RA patients was 6.1 per 1000 person-years, which was 2.4 times higher than the rate in non-RA patients [N1-F1]. After adjustment for VTE risk factors such as CVD, surgery, hospitalization, medications, and acute phase reactants, the hazard ratio remained elevated at 1.4 (95% CI 1.1–1.7) [N1-F1]. A later study comparing RA with non-RA populations found an even higher hazard ratio of 2.2 for DVT and 2.7 for PE compared with non-RA patients, with the overall VTE hazard ratio still elevated after adjustment [N1-F1]. The evidence base also notes that RA is associated with a two-fold increased risk of VTE compared with the general population in some reports [N1-R3][N1-R4].

The most strongly linked RA features are disease activity, chronic inflammation, and comorbid conditions. The RA-VTE review study found that VTE risk increased with increasing RA disease activity, from 0.52% following visits in remission to 1.08% following visits with active disease [N8-R2]. A separate review also states that RA is associated with chronic inflammation, which is likely to underlie the association with VTE [N5-R4]. The evidence further notes that established VTE risk factors such as age, immobilization, and comorbid conditions occur more frequently in RA patients [N5-R3]. The RA-VTE cohort also found that one-third of VTE cases had at least one major VTE risk factor within 90 days before or after the event, including recent hospitalization, surgery, and malignancy [N1-F1]. This indicates that disease activity and associated comorbidities are major drivers of RA-related VTE risk [N8-R2][N5-R4][N5-R3].

How risk changes over time from diagnosis onward is less precisely quantified, but the evidence suggests that risk remains elevated over follow-up. The RA-VTE cohort followed patients over a mean of 2 years and found persistent elevated risk after adjustment for various factors [N1-F1]. Another study reported that within a median of 5.8 years after initial diagnosis, the rate of VTE occurrence was 4.5 per 1000 person-years [N8-R5]. This implies that the risk does not fall to a normal level shortly after diagnosis and may remain present across years of follow-up. The evidence also supports a role for time since diagnosis and treatment status in shaping risk, as several studies explicitly examined time since diagnosis and treatment effects [N8-R1][N8-R2][N8-R5].

Overall, RA is associated with a baseline VTE risk that is consistently higher than controls, with disease activity, chronic inflammation, and comorbid conditions being the most strongly linked features [N1-F1][N8-R2][N5-R4]. The risk does not appear to normalize quickly after diagnosis and may persist over years of follow-up [N1-F1][N8-R5]. The evidence here is strongest for relative risk and for disease activity, while the absolute time-course from diagnosis onward is supported but less precisely measured in the provided sources.

Clinical management and prevention implications

The evidence supports a staged approach to VTE prevention after rheumatoid arthritis (RA) diagnosis and hospitalization. Thromboprophylaxis should be indicated when the risk of VTE is elevated, especially during acute hospitalization and in the early post-discharge period, because both settings carry a strong risk of VTE. The MITH study showed that hospitalization itself was associated with a 38-fold increased hazard of VTE, with risk remaining 3-fold higher up to 3 months after discharge [N2-F2]. For hospitalized RA patients, additional risk factors include inflammation, immobilization, comorbid conditions, and treatment-related exposures [N4-R4][N5-R4][N5-R3]. This means that prophylaxis should be targeted at high-risk patients rather than assumed for all patients.

Guidance on duration and type of prophylaxis suggests that in-hospital prophylaxis is appropriate, but post-discharge prophylaxis should be risk-adapted. The MITH study found that during hospitalization the risk was highest, then declined over the first few months after discharge [N2-F2]. The general VTE literature also notes that hospital-acquired VTE is often defined as VTE occurring during or within 3 months after hospitalization [N6-R4]. This supports the idea that thromboprophylaxis should cover the acute hospital stay and the early post-discharge period, but not necessarily be extended indefinitely. The AHA statement emphasizes that for patients at high or moderate risk, pharmacological or mechanical prophylaxis is recommended over no prophylaxis, while for patients at low risk, the evidence is less clear [N4-R5]. In hospitalized RA patients, where risk is amplified by inflammation and comorbidities, the threshold for pharmacological prophylaxis is likely lower.

The evidence also implies that prophylaxis should be tailored to the patient’s risk profile. Hospitalized RA patients have multiple risk drivers, including recent hospitalization, immobilization, comorbid conditions, and RA-related inflammation [N4-R4][N5-R4][N5-R3]. The post-hospitalization follow-up evidence further shows that recurrence risk is highest in the first few weeks and months after discharge, with long-term recurrence continuing for years [N3-F3][N3-R5][N7-R5]. This means that risk stratification should not be static. After discharge, patients should be reassessed for ongoing risk factors, including continued inflammation, mobility, comorbidity, and treatment burden, rather than treated as if the risk has returned to baseline [N5-R4][N5-R3][N3-F3].

How risk stratification should be adapted over time is best viewed as a continuum: acute hospitalization is a high-risk period, the first few months after discharge are a moderate-to-high recurrence risk period, and beyond 1 year the risk remains substantial, with recurrence continuing for decades in some cohorts [N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R5][N7-R5]. Therefore, management should shift from acute prophylaxis during hospitalization to risk-based follow-up after discharge. For hospitalized RA patients, this means using hospitalization, immobilization, comorbid conditions, and disease activity to identify those most likely to benefit from continued prophylaxis or monitoring [N4-R4][N5-R3][N8-R2]. The evidence also supports the importance of identifying patients with persistent risk factors such as active disease or ongoing inflammation, because these are associated with higher VTE risk [N8-R2][N5-R4].

In summary, thromboprophylaxis is indicated during hospitalization and should continue into the early post-discharge period because VTE risk remains elevated for at least 3 months after discharge [N2-F2][N6-R4]. The duration and type of prophylaxis should be guided by risk stratification, with pharmacological or mechanical prophylaxis favored in higher-risk hospitalized RA patients [N4-R5]. Over time, risk stratification should be adapted to changing clinical circumstances: acute hospitalization is high-risk, the first few months after discharge are a recurrence-prone period, and longer-term management should account for continued inflammation, comorbidities, and treatment status [N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R5][N5-R4][N8-R2].

## Overall conclusion

The risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) changes over time after a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and subsequent hospitalization in a clear, stage-specific pattern. The risk is highest during hospitalization itself, then declines sharply but remains elevated for at least months after discharge, and continues to carry substantial long-term recurrence risk for years. For RA patients, disease activity and inflammation are major drivers of baseline VTE risk, while hospitalization, immobilization, and comorbidities amplify that risk further. Management should therefore be staged: acute hospitalization is the highest-risk period, the first few months after discharge are a recurrence-prone window, and longer-term care should remain attentive to continued inflammation and risk factors [N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R5][N8-R2].

## 1) Baseline VTE risk associated with RA

RA is associated with an elevated baseline VTE risk compared with controls. The evidence shows that RA patients have a higher incidence rate of VTE than non-RA patients, with relative risk estimates ranging from elevated after adjustment for VTE risk factors to even higher estimates for DVT and PE in some studies [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. One large cohort study found that RA was associated with a hazard ratio of 1.4 for VTE after adjustment for major VTE risk factors such as hospitalization, surgery, and malignancy, and even higher hazard ratios for DVT and PE [N1-F1]. Another review noted that RA is associated with a two-fold increased risk of VTE compared with the general population [N1-R3][N1-R4].

The strongest RA features linked to VTE are disease activity and chronic inflammation. The RA-VTE review found that VTE risk increased with increasing RA disease activity, from 0.52% following visits in remission to 1.08% following visits with active disease [N8-R2]. A separate review states that RA is associated with chronic inflammation, which is likely to underlie the association with VTE [N5-R4]. Established VTE risk factors such as age, immobilization, and comorbid conditions also occur more frequently in RA patients [N5-R3]. This means that RA-related inflammation and comorbid disease burden are major drivers of baseline VTE risk, not just hospitalization alone [N5-R4][N5-R3][N8-R2].

## 2) Acute hospitalization-related VTE risk and timing

Hospitalization itself is a major acute trigger for VTE. The MITH study found that hospitalization was associated with a 38-fold increased hazard of VTE compared with not recently hospitalized individuals, and the risk remained 3-fold higher up to 3 months after discharge [N2-F2]. During hospital stay, the risk is especially high: the VTE rate was 71.8 per 1000 person-years during hospitalization, versus 1.4 per 1000 person-years in the non-recency hospitalized comparator group [N2-F2]. Over the first few months after discharge, the risk declines progressively: 35.1 per 1000 person-years in the first month, 11.3 per 1000 person-years in the second month, and 5.2 per 1000 person-years in the third month [N2-F2]. So the risk peaks early and declines over time, but not back to baseline [N2-F2].

For hospitalized RA patients, the risk is further amplified by several factors. The evidence notes that RA-related inflammation, immobilization, and comorbid conditions are important risk factors [N5-R4][N5-R3]. The general VTE prevention guidance also highlights that hospitalization with immobilization and comorbidities can increase VTE risk [N4-R4]. In hospitalized RA patients, RA-related inflammation and treatment burden make the hospital stay a particularly high-risk period [N4-R4][N5-R4][N5-R3].

## 3) Post-hospitalization follow-up and long-term VTE risk

The evidence shows that VTE risk does not end with discharge. After hospitalization, the risk remains elevated for weeks and months, and recurrence risk is notably higher in the first few weeks/months after discharge [N3-F3][N3-R5]. The Tromsø study found that recurrence risk was highest during the first 6–12 months after the first VTE event [N3-F3]. A separate study found that recurrence risk was at least 6% within 2 years and continued to recur for at least 10 years after the first VTE [N7-R1]. The AFP review also reports that one third of people with a VTE will have a recurrence within 10 years, and one third to one half will have a recurrence after a DVT [N3-R5]. This means the early post-discharge period is not the only concern; recurrence risk persists for years.

Beyond 1 year, the long-term risk continues to accumulate and may plateau or remain substantial. The AFP review states that recurrence risk is highest during the first 6–12 months and continues for at least 10 years after the initial event [N3-R5]. A 2020 study on recurrence after a first venous thromboembolic event found cumulative recurrence probabilities of 10.9% after 2 years, 29% after 10 years, and 56% after 20 years [N7-R5]. This indicates that long-term risk is substantial and may not simply decline sharply after the first year [N7-R5]. The evidence also suggests that recurrence risk may plateau or remain elevated over decades, rather than falling to a negligible baseline [N7-R5].

## 4) Impact of continued inflammation, treatment, and lifestyle factors

Continued inflammation, treatment, and lifestyle factors all play a role in shaping VTE risk after RA and hospitalization. The evidence on RA and VTE indicates that chronic inflammation is likely a major contributor to the association between RA and VTE [N5-R4]. Hospitalized RA patients face risk factors linked to inflammation, immobilization, and comorbid conditions [N5-R3][N5-R4]. The general VTE literature also emphasizes that recurrence risk depends on the clinical characteristics of the initial event, with persistent risk factors such as active cancer associated with higher recurrence [N3-F3]. In the context of post-hospitalization follow-up, this means that inflammation, treatment burden, comorbid conditions, and lifestyle factors may all contribute to ongoing risk [N5-R4][N5-R3][N3-F3].

For RA patients specifically, continued disease activity is associated with higher VTE risk [N8-R2]. This supports the idea that VTE risk is not a one-time event but a dynamic process influenced by the patient’s inflammatory state and treatment response [N8-R2][N5-R4].

## 5) Clinical management and prevention implications

Clinical management should be staged. Thromboprophylaxis is indicated during hospitalization and should continue into the early post-discharge period because VTE risk remains elevated for at least 3 months after discharge [N2-F2][N6-R4]. The MITH study’s findings support a strong rationale for prophylaxis during hospitalization and the immediate post-discharge period [N2-F2]. The general VTE prevention guidance also emphasizes that for patients at high or moderate risk, pharmacological or mechanical prophylaxis is recommended over no prophylaxis [N4-R5].

Guidance on duration and type of prophylaxis suggests that in-hospital prophylaxis is appropriate, but post-discharge prophylaxis should be risk-adapted. The evidence supports the idea that hospital-acquired VTE is often defined as VTE occurring during or within 3 months after hospitalization [N6-R4]. This suggests that thromboprophylaxis should cover the acute hospital stay and the early post-discharge period, but not necessarily be extended indefinitely [N2-F2][N6-R4]. The AHA statement also notes that extending thromboprophylaxis after discharge may not provide clinical benefit and may increase bleeding risk [N4-R5]. Therefore, prophylaxis should be guided by risk stratification rather than assumed for all patients [N4-R5].

Risk stratification should be adapted over time. Hospitalized RA patients have multiple risk drivers, including recent hospitalization, immobilization, comorbid conditions, and RA-related inflammation [N4-R4][N5-R3][N5-R4]. The post-hospitalization follow-up evidence further shows that recurrence risk is highest in the first few weeks and months after discharge, with long-term recurrence continuing for years [N3-F3][N3-R5][N7-R5]. This means that risk stratification should not be static. After discharge, patients should be reassessed for ongoing risk factors, including continued inflammation, mobility, comorbidity, and treatment burden, rather than treated as if the risk has returned to baseline [N5-R4][N5-R3][N3-F3].

## 6) Practical summary of how VTE risk changes over time

If you want a simple timeline:

1. **At RA diagnosis and in the general RA population**: baseline VTE risk is elevated, with disease activity and chronic inflammation being the strongest drivers [N1-F1][N8-R2][N5-R4].
2. **During hospitalization**: risk rises sharply, with hospitalization associated with a 38-fold increased hazard of VTE and a 3-fold higher risk up to 3 months after discharge [N2-F2].
3. **Immediately after discharge**: risk declines but remains elevated; the first few weeks and months are a high-recurrence period [N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R5].
4. **Beyond 1 year**: long-term recurrence risk continues and may plateau or accumulate over years, with recurrence probabilities reaching at least 6% within 2 years and continuing for decades [N7-R1][N3-R5][N7-R5].
5. **Over time**: management should shift from acute hospital prophylaxis to risk-based follow-up, with continued attention to inflammation, comorbidities, and treatment burden [N4-R4][N5-R3][N8-R2].

## Bottom line

After RA and hospitalization, VTE risk follows a predictable but prolonged trajectory: it is highest during hospitalization, then declines sharply but remains elevated for months after discharge, and continues to carry substantial long-term recurrence risk for years. RA-related inflammation and disease activity are major baseline drivers of VTE risk, while hospitalization, immobilization, and comorbidities further amplify the risk during hospital stays and early follow-up [N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R5][N8-R2][N5-R4]. Clinical management should therefore be staged, with prophylaxis targeted to high-risk patients during hospitalization and the early post-discharge period, and risk stratification adapted over time to changing clinical circumstances [N4-R4][N4-R5][N5-R3].

## Overall conclusion

The risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) changes over time after a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and subsequent hospitalization in a clear, stage-specific pattern. The risk is highest during hospitalization itself, then declines sharply but remains elevated for at least months after discharge, and continues to carry substantial long-term recurrence risk for years. For RA patients, disease activity and inflammation are major drivers of baseline VTE risk, while hospitalization, immobilization, and comorbidities amplify that risk further. Management should therefore be staged: acute hospitalization is the highest-risk period, the first few months after discharge are a recurrence-prone window, and longer-term care should remain attentive to continued inflammation and risk factors [N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R5][N8-R2].

## 1) Baseline VTE risk associated with RA

RA is associated with an elevated baseline VTE risk compared with controls. The evidence shows that RA patients have a higher incidence rate of VTE than non-RA patients, with relative risk estimates ranging from elevated after adjustment for VTE risk factors to even higher estimates for DVT and PE in some studies [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. One large cohort study found that RA was associated with a hazard ratio of 1.4 for VTE after adjustment for major VTE risk factors such as hospitalization, surgery, and malignancy, and even higher hazard ratios for DVT and PE [N1-F1]. Another review noted that RA is associated with a two-fold increased risk of VTE compared with the general population [N1-R3][N1-R4].

The strongest RA features linked to VTE are disease activity and chronic inflammation. The RA-VTE review found that VTE risk increased with increasing RA disease activity, from 0.52% following visits in remission to 1.08% following visits with active disease [N8-R2]. A separate review states that RA is associated with chronic inflammation, which is likely to underlie the association with VTE [N5-R4]. Established VTE risk factors such as age, immobilization, and comorbid conditions also occur more frequently in RA patients [N5-R3]. This means that RA-related inflammation and comorbid disease burden are major drivers of baseline VTE risk, not just hospitalization alone [N5-R4][N5-R3][N8-R2].

## 2) Acute hospitalization-related VTE risk and timing

Hospitalization itself is a major acute trigger for VTE. The MITH study found that hospitalization was associated with a 38-fold increased hazard of VTE compared with not recently hospitalized individuals, and the risk remained 3-fold higher up to 3 months after discharge [N2-F2]. During hospital stay, the risk is especially high: the VTE rate was 71.8 per 1000 person-years during hospitalization, versus 1.4 per 1000 person-years in the non-recency hospitalized comparator group [N2-F2]. Over the first few months after discharge, the risk declines progressively: 35.1 per 1000 person-years in the first month, 11.3 per 1000 person-years in the second month, and 5.2 per 1000 person-years in the third month [N2-F2]. So the risk peaks early and declines over time, but not back to baseline [N2-F2].

For hospitalized RA patients, the risk is further amplified by several factors. The evidence notes that RA-related inflammation, immobilization, and comorbid conditions are important risk factors [N5-R4][N5-R3]. The general VTE prevention guidance also highlights that hospitalization with immobilization and comorbidities can increase VTE risk [N4-R4]. In hospitalized RA patients, RA-related inflammation and treatment burden make the hospital stay a particularly high-risk period [N4-R4][N5-R4][N5-R3].

## 3) Post-hospitalization follow-up and long-term VTE risk

The evidence shows that VTE risk does not end with discharge. After hospitalization, the risk remains elevated for weeks and months, and recurrence risk is notably higher in the first few weeks/months after discharge [N3-F3][N3-R5]. The Tromsø study found that recurrence risk was highest during the first 6–12 months after the first VTE event [N3-F3]. A separate study found that recurrence risk was at least 6% within 2 years and continued to recur for at least 10 years after the first VTE [N7-R1]. The AFP review also reports that one third of people with a VTE will have a recurrence within 10 years, and one third to one half will have a recurrence after a DVT [N3-R5]. This means the early post-discharge period is not the only concern; recurrence risk persists for years.

The AFP review states that recurrence risk is highest during the first 6–12 months and continues for at least 10 years after the initial event [N3-R5]. A 2020 study on recurrence after a first venous thromboembolic event found cumulative recurrence probabilities of 10.9% after 2 years, 29% after 10 years, and 56% after 20 years [N7-R5]. This indicates that long-term risk is substantial and may not simply decline sharply after the first year [N7-R5]. The evidence also suggests that recurrence risk may plateau or remain elevated over decades, rather than falling to a negligible baseline [N7-R5].

Continued inflammation, treatment, and lifestyle factors all play a role in shaping VTE risk after RA and hospitalization. ## 5) Clinical management and prevention implications

Clinical management should be staged. Thromboprophylaxis is indicated during hospitalization and should continue into the early post-discharge period because VTE risk remains elevated for at least 3 months after discharge [N2-F2][N6-R4]. The post-hospitalization follow-up evidence further shows that recurrence risk is highest in the first few weeks and months after discharge, with long-term recurrence continuing for years [N3-F3][N3-R5][N7-R5]. This means that risk stratification should not be static. After discharge, patients should be reassessed for ongoing risk factors, including continued inflammation, mobility, comorbidity, and treatment burden, rather than treated as if the risk has returned to baseline [N5-R4][N5-R3][N3-F3].

## 6) Practical summary of how VTE risk changes over time

If you want a simple timeline:

1. **At RA diagnosis and in the general RA population**: baseline VTE risk is elevated, with disease activity and chronic inflammation being the strongest drivers [N1-F1][N8-R2][N5-R4].
2. **During hospitalization**: risk rises sharply, with hospitalization associated with a 38-fold increased hazard of VTE and a 3-fold higher risk up to 3 months after discharge [N2-F2].
3. **Immediately after discharge**: risk declines but remains elevated; the first few weeks and months are a high-recurrence period [N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R5].
4. **Beyond 1 year**: long-term recurrence risk continues and may plateau or accumulate over years, with recurrence probabilities reaching at least 6% within 2 years and continuing for decades [N7-R1][N3-R5][N7-R5].
5. **Over time**: management should shift from acute hospital prophylaxis to risk-based follow-up, with continued attention to inflammation, comorbidities, and treatment burden [N4-R4][N5-R3][N8-R2].

## Bottom line

After RA and hospitalization, VTE risk follows a predictable but prolonged trajectory: it is highest during hospitalization, then declines sharply but remains elevated for months after discharge, and continues to carry substantial long-term recurrence risk for years. RA-related inflammation and disease activity are major baseline drivers of VTE risk, while hospitalization, immobilization, and comorbidities further amplify the risk during hospital stays and early follow-up [N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R5][N8-R2][N5-R4].
